[1] XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant") is a citizen of Hungary. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division ("RAD") to set aside the RPD decision and to find that she is a Convention refugee and/or a person in need of protection pursuant to the IRPA.

[2] The Appellant has tendered no new evidence under either subsection 110(4) of the IRPA or Rule 29 of the RAD Rules.2
DETERMINATION

[3] I hereby confirm the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee under section 96 of the IRPA, nor is she a person in need of protection within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Accordingly, this appeal is denied.

BACKGROUND

[4] The Appellant is a Hungarian national who is of Roma ethnicity. Her allegations are set out at some length in her original Basis of Claim ("BOC") Narrative,3 as well as the Amended BOC Narrative dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019.4 Essentially, her claim is two-fold:
(i) as a Roma individual in Hungary, she claims to have experienced long-term discrimination and fear of violence which amounts to persecution; and
(ii) fear of gender-based violence at the hands of her former partner, "G.S.".
ROLE OF THE RAD

[5] My role is to review the RPD decision on a standard of correctness after having conducted an independent examination of the evidence.5 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard or documentary evidence tendered at the hearing which may, in certain cases, allow me to defer to RPD findings. I do not believe the RPD enjoyed any such meaningful advantage in this matter, so no deference will be accorded and all evidence from the RPD hearing has been considered in arriving at my decision.

[11] As previously indicated, the Appellant's claim appears to be at an intersection point between her claim of discrimination amounting to persecution, based upon her membership in the Hungarian-Roma community, and a claim as a Hungarian woman facing gender-related persecution at the hands of a former partner. Although gender is not specifically enumerated as a Convention ground, the definition of a Convention refugee may properly be interpreted as providing protection for women who demonstrate a well-founded fear of gender-related persecution by reason of any one, or combination of, enumerated grounds such as, for example, membership in a particular social group. Gender is an innate characteristic and may form a particular social group. According to the Guideline, the real issue is whether the violence - experienced or feared - is a serious violation of a fundamental human right on a Convention ground and in what circumstances can the risk of that violence be said to result from a failure of state protection.

[12] The Appellant argues that implementation of the Guideline requires a "loosening" of evidentiary considerations. With respect, I disagree with this notion and, instead, read Guideline 4 as establishing a principled approach which an Immigration and Refugee Board ("IRB") decision-maker should consider in arriving at a decision that truly incorporates the spirit and letter of the Guideline and is fair to the claimant, yet maintains the integrity of the refugee system.

[14] In my view, the Guideline does not promote or mandate a relaxation of the evidentiary standard that a claimant who falls within its ambit must meet to establish her claim. The Guideline is not a shield which prevents a claimant's evidence from being tested; so, for example, evidence which lacks credibility is not rehabilitated by resort to the Guideline but still requires IRB decision- makers to conduct the hearing, and to analyze the claim and the evidence in support of the claim in a manner that is consistent with its principles. [16] Based upon the foregoing, I find that the RPD conducted both the hearing and rendered its decision in a manner that demonstrated engagement and consistency with the Guideline.
The Appellant's credibility issues

[17] As noted by the RPD, the starting point of any credibility analysis is the presumption of truthfulness which arises from the Maldonado decision9 which stands for the proposition that where an applicant swears to the truth of certain allegations, this creates a presumption of truthfulness that the allegations are true unless there be reason to doubt their truthfulness. This presumption is always rebuttable and may be rebutted by an accumulation of inconsistencies, omissions and contradictions. For reasons which follow, I concur with the RPD that the allegations advanced by the Appellant had significant credibility concerns which undermined her allegations.
Failure to disclose flight from Hungary and seven months' stay in the United States of America ("USA") is a material omission

[18] The Appellant failed to disclose that she left Hungary in XXXX of 2012 and stayed with a friend in Brooklyn, New York, USA, for a period of approximately seven months. This omission only came to light upon the Minister's intervention. I might add that upon the Minister's intervention, it was determined that one of the incidents of persecution could not have occurred as alleged by the Appellant as she would have been in the USA at the time. Following the Minister's intervention, the Appellant filed an amended BOC narrative in which she claimed that the date of the incident as set out in the original intake documents was incorrect. This amendment and the explanation were accepted by the RPD as an honest error. However, the RPD did find that the omission of her 2012 trip to the USA and her subsequent return to Hungary in XXXX of 2013 was significant and undermined her overall credibility. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in determining that she was not credible based on minor omissions that were not material to her claim. I am not persuaded by this argument and, in my view, omission of what she alleges was a flight from Hungary due to persecution, subsequently returning from a safe haven to the country of origin where the persecution occurred is not a minor omission and relates to the fundamental underpinning of her claim.

[19] The Appellant alleges that she failed to disclose this information on the advice of former counsel. In rejecting this explanation, the RPD noted that she was represented by experienced counsel who would have been well aware of the biometrics information routinely shared between Canada and the USA Department of Homeland Security and that this error would have eventually come to light. Further to that, I note that there is no evidence that former counsel has been put on notice that such advice might have compromised the Appellant's claim, nor has there been any evidence adduced regarding any form of complaint to the Law Society of Ontario or, for that matter, even to the IRB regarding former counsel's conduct. The Appellant argues that competent and experienced counsel does not necessarily equate to "principled", but allegations such as this are serious and, if accurate, strike at the core of the integrity of the refugee protection system. In the absence of any such evidence regarding former counsel's conduct, I agree with the RPD finding and find it correct that the Appellant's failure to disclose her 7 months' stay in the USA was based on advice from her former counsel undermines her credibility and the credibility of her claim.

[22] Other than general country condition type documents, there is little evidence that is corroborative of the specific allegations made in this claim. On the issue of corroboration, I note that the Federal Court in Senadheerage began its analysis with the traditional view that the law of evidence does not require testimony to be corroborated by written documents.18 In Senadheerage, Mr. Justice Grammond points out that the IRB (with good reason) often requires asylum claimants to corroborate their claim with written evidence.19 Reasons for corroboration vary but are rooted in the notion that it is difficult for the Canadian government to investigate events that occurred in another country and requiring corroboration helps ensure that refugee protection is granted to those who deserve it.20 While there are instances and events which may preclude or prevent the gathering of corroborative evidence, " [...] requiring corroboration may be a manner of granting 'fair consideration to those who come to Canada claiming persecution' while 'maintaining the integrity of the Canadian refugee protection system [...]'".21 In making these statements, the Court cautioned that any requirement for corroboration must be "properly calibrated" to avoid putting refugee claimants in an impossible situation.22

[23] The Federal Court also noted that the absence of a general requirement for corroboration is considered a corollary of the Maldonado presumption of truthfulness discussed above which, of course, stands for the proposition that when an applicant swears to the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there be reason to doubt their truthfulness. [48] In reviewing the documentary evidence, I note that since 2013, the situation has improved for Roma citizens of Hungary;51 the reform is progressing, and positive change has been instituted with concrete results having been achieved. Mindful of my task to differentiate between good intentions or "serious efforts" and actual results, I note that concrete results have been achieved, although it is clear that the pace of these reforms has come under some criticism. For example, the NDP establishes the following:
(i) the European Court of Human Rights ruling that Hungary discriminated against Roma persons when police failed to investigate a 2012 racist attack.52 Once again, as discussed above (and as analyzed by the Federal Court in Burai), decisions such as this represent a positive trend and are concrete results in establishing the operational adequacy of state protection;
(ii) in July 2016, the Hungarian Police, in conjunction with the "Fraternal Association of European Roma Law Enforcement Officers," (an association which aims to promote equal opportunities in law enforcement and to reduce prejudice between law enforcement and Roma Communities),53 initiated a project called "Initiative for the Improvement of the Police Prevention and Handling of Hate Incidents" which resulted in Hungarian police officers from each county receiving specialized training on responding to and investigating hate crimes;54
(iii) a comprehensive complaints process against police and other officials providing government services has been instituted. Although initial complaints are dealt with by the police agency, they can be escalated to an Independent Police Complaints Board. According to the NDP, in the first 9 months of 2014, over 4,000 officers were subject to discipline ranging from imprisonment in the most egregious cases to dismissal to fines and other penalties for less serious offences;55
(iv) the Equal Treatment Authority ("ETA") and the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights are independent bodies established by the Hungarian government. They are tasked with a mandate to receive and deal with individual and public complaints about unequal treatment and ensuring the protection of fundamental rights, respectively. As set out in the NDP, the ETA is active in soliciting complaints and was instrumental in legal action against the city of Miskolc regarding housing discrimination against Roma persons;56
(v) there has been a dedicated effort made in the form of outreach programs designed to recruit police officers from the Roma community and to encourage Roma youth to consider law enforcement as a career. In addition to such recruitment and outreach programs, there have been scholarships granted to Roma youth interested in law enforcement careers, as well as a broad array of other scholarship opportunities for Roma students arising from the National Social Inclusion Policy;57
(vi) legal assistance and support are available for victims of human rights violations and hate crimes;58
(vii) the Equal Treatment Authority ruled in favour of a Romani woman who was harassed with ethnic slurs by hospital staff while giving birth and the hospital was required to publicize the birth and pay a fine;59
(viii) while there are widespread reports of segregation of Roma students in Hungarian schools, the NDP reports that the Metropolitan Court of Budapest delivered a decision that established that the ministry in charge of education was directly responsible for segregation and was ordered to desegregate. subthemes.text: [53] As discussed above, the Appellant's claim features an intersectionality between her claim as a Hungarian Roma and her claim as a Hungarian Roma woman claiming gender-related persecution at the hands of her former partner. Though it is not possible to neatly dissect the two aspects of her claim as there is a certain degree of overlap, it can be notionally segmented into two distinct phases: the first phase being prior to her departure from Hungary for the USA in 2012 and the second phase commencing with her subsequent return in 2013. Her failure to claim refugee status in the USA and her return to Hungary has been found to undermine the subjective fear element necessary to support a successful refugee claim, particularly with events that pre-dated her departure from her country of origin. Following re-availment to Hungary, she became involved with her partner, "G.S." who she claims became abusive to her because of her Roma ethnicity. The evidence featured a number of credibility concerns that have been highlighted and which cast doubt upon the credibility of her claim. While corroborative material may have been readily available in the form of medical reports relating to particular incidents, none was provided, and the Appellant provided unreasonable and/or inconsistent and evolving explanations for not having such reports which resulted in adverse credibility findings. Such corroborative material that was provided could not be given any evidentiary weight due to reliability concerns. In addition, the Appellant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the incidents involving "G.S." occurred. The Appellant has the onus to provide clear and convincing evidence that adequate state protection is unavailable to her and, on a balance of probabilities, has failed to do so.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant") is a citizen of Hungary. She appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division ("RPD") in the redetermination of her claim dated November 25, 2019, whereby the RPD found that she was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 ("IRPA"). The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division ("RAD") to set aside the RPD decision and to find that she is a Convention refugee and/or a person in need of protection pursuant to the IRPA.

[2] The Appellant has tendered no new evidence under either subsection 110(4) of the IRPA or Rule 29 of the RAD Rules.2
DETERMINATION

[3] I hereby confirm the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee under section 96 of the IRPA, nor is she a person in need of protection within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Accordingly, this appeal is denied.
BACKGROUND

[4] The Appellant is a Hungarian national who is of Roma ethnicity. Her allegations are set out at some length in her original Basis of Claim ("BOC") Narrative,3 as well as the Amended BOC Narrative dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019.4 Essentially, her claim is two-fold:
(i) as a Roma individual in Hungary, she claims to have experienced long-term discrimination and fear of violence which amounts to persecution; and
(ii) fear of gender-based violence at the hands of her former partner, "G.S.".
ROLE OF THE RAD

[5] My role is to review the RPD decision on a standard of correctness after having conducted an independent examination of the evidence.5 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard or documentary evidence tendered at the hearing which may, in certain cases, allow me to defer to RPD findings. I do not believe the RPD enjoyed any such meaningful advantage in this matter, so no deference will be accorded and all evidence from the RPD hearing has been considered in arriving at my decision.
ANALYSIS OF MERITS OF APPEAL

[6] The Appellant's identity as a Hungarian national was established to the satisfaction of the RPD with the production of a valid Hungarian passport; her ethnicity as a Roma was established based upon her testimony and a confirmation letter from a member of the Roma Nationality Self-Government of the Settlement of Megyaszo.6 I confirm and accept those findings are correct.
The RPD Decision and the Appellant's allegation of error on the part of the panel

[7] Following its analysis, the RPD concluded that the Appellant had failed to provide reliable evidence to establish essential elements of her claim and that, on a balance of probabilities, her testimony on material aspects of the claim was not credible which undermined her overall credibility. Moreover, the panel found that there were significant credibility concerns which undermined the Appellant's allegations regarding the alleged persecution she would face if returned to Hungary. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred as follows:
(i) the RPD failed to adequately consider and apply IRB Chairperson's Guideline 4 for Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Based Persecution (the "Guideline");7
(ii) the RPD erred in determining the Appellant was not credible based on minor omissions that were not material to her claim;
(iii) the RPD erred in determining that the Appellant's failure to claim refugee status in the United States was indicative of a lack of subjective fear;
(iv) the RPD failed to engage in a forward-looking analysis of the risk faced by the Appellant if returned to Hungary; and
(v) the RPD failed to conduct an analysis of whether state protection would be forthcoming if the Appellant returned to Hungary.
Did the RPD meaningfully engage with "Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution"?

[8] The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to acknowledge the persecution she had faced as a woman enduring domestic abuse and imposed an evidentiary standard that was not in keeping with the Guideline. In addition, the Appellant argues that while the RPD referenced the Guideline in its reasons, the decision did not display engagement with the Guideline in a meaningful way.

[9] I disagree with counsel's submission. While counsel is correct in noting that the Reasons clearly reference the Guideline yet provide no specific formal analysis of its application or impact (if any) on the decision, for reasons which follow, I find that the hearing was conducted through the lens of Guideline 4 and the Reasons which followed are, likewise, consistent with and apply the objectives stated therein.

[10] In conducting my independent assessment of this matter, in addition to reading the transcript of the proceeding, I have listened to the audiotape of the hearing and confirm that, as indicated in the RPD Reasons, the hearing was conducted in a sensitive manner, with the member asking all questions in a calm, non-confrontational and respectful tone of voice. From the outset, the RPD made it clear to all that sensitive issues might arise during the hearing and requested both counsel8 to conduct questioning in a sensitive and understanding manner. Furthermore, the RPD member spent time at the beginning of the hearing and acknowledged that the Appellant might be under stress and may have difficulty in recalling exact dates. In my view, the RPD member exuded a calm and reassuring presence throughout the hearing and, at no time, did counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant express any concern regarding the manner in which the hearing was conducted. Although the Appellant testified with the assistance of an interpreter, I paid special attention to the tone of her voice as she testified and, apart from one instance where she became somewhat emotional in discussing her grandson's autism, she displayed no signs of stress or emotion and delivered her testimony in a calm and subdued tone of voice. A break was offered at an appropriate stage of the proceeding, the duration of which was shortened on the request of the Appellant's counsel. I believe that it is reasonable to infer from counsel's request for a shorter break that he, too, observed no signs of stress or relived trauma in his client. I could discern no such indications from having listened to the hearing tape and, in short, I find that the conduct of the hearing was entirely consistent with the Guideline.

[11] As previously indicated, the Appellant's claim appears to be at an intersection point between her claim of discrimination amounting to persecution, based upon her membership in the Hungarian-Roma community, and a claim as a Hungarian woman facing gender-related persecution at the hands of a former partner. Although gender is not specifically enumerated as a Convention ground, the definition of a Convention refugee may properly be interpreted as providing protection for women who demonstrate a well-founded fear of gender-related persecution by reason of any one, or combination of, enumerated grounds such as, for example, membership in a particular social group. Gender is an innate characteristic and may form a particular social group. According to the Guideline, the real issue is whether the violence - experienced or feared - is a serious violation of a fundamental human right on a Convention ground and in what circumstances can the risk of that violence be said to result from a failure of state protection.

[12] The Appellant argues that implementation of the Guideline requires a "loosening" of evidentiary considerations. With respect, I disagree with this notion and, instead, read Guideline 4 as establishing a principled approach which an Immigration and Refugee Board ("IRB") decision-maker should consider in arriving at a decision that truly incorporates the spirit and letter of the Guideline and is fair to the claimant, yet maintains the integrity of the refugee system.

[14] In my view, the Guideline does not promote or mandate a relaxation of the evidentiary standard that a claimant who falls within its ambit must meet to establish her claim. The Guideline is not a shield which prevents a claimant's evidence from being tested; so, for example, evidence which lacks credibility is not rehabilitated by resort to the Guideline but still requires IRB decision- makers to conduct the hearing, and to analyze the claim and the evidence in support of the claim in a manner that is consistent with its principles. My interpretation of the Guideline is that it advocates and establishes a commitment on the part of the IRB and its decision-makers to sensitive handling of claimants who allege gender-related abuse and awareness of certain evidentiary considerations that may be missing or difficult to obtain in such cases - to be balanced however with the fundamentals of the refugee process requiring proof to certain standards and credibly establishing a well-founded fear of persecution or being a person in need of protection.

[15] Furthermore, the Appellant alleges that the RPD particularly erred in dismissing the letter provided by the Appellant's mother without engaging in any attempt to ascertain its veracity. I disagree. While it may have been within the RPD member's ability to contact the mother, on its face, this letter is not credible and, in my view, it was open to the panel to assign it no weight. I discuss the mother's letter in greater detail below with respect to the Appellant's credibility issues.

[16] Based upon the foregoing, I find that the RPD conducted both the hearing and rendered its decision in a manner that demonstrated engagement and consistency with the Guideline.
The Appellant's credibility issues

[17] As noted by the RPD, the starting point of any credibility analysis is the presumption of truthfulness which arises from the Maldonado decision9 which stands for the proposition that where an applicant swears to the truth of certain allegations, this creates a presumption of truthfulness that the allegations are true unless there be reason to doubt their truthfulness. This presumption is always rebuttable and may be rebutted by an accumulation of inconsistencies, omissions and contradictions. For reasons which follow, I concur with the RPD that the allegations advanced by the Appellant had significant credibility concerns which undermined her allegations.
Failure to disclose flight from Hungary and seven months' stay in the United States of America ("USA") is a material omission

[18] The Appellant failed to disclose that she left Hungary in XXXX of 2012 and stayed with a friend in Brooklyn, New York, USA, for a period of approximately seven months. This omission only came to light upon the Minister's intervention. I might add that upon the Minister's intervention, it was determined that one of the incidents of persecution could not have occurred as alleged by the Appellant as she would have been in the USA at the time. Following the Minister's intervention, the Appellant filed an amended BOC narrative in which she claimed that the date of the incident as set out in the original intake documents was incorrect. This amendment and the explanation were accepted by the RPD as an honest error. However, the RPD did find that the omission of her 2012 trip to the USA and her subsequent return to Hungary in XXXX of 2013 was significant and undermined her overall credibility. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in determining that she was not credible based on minor omissions that were not material to her claim. I am not persuaded by this argument and, in my view, omission of what she alleges was a flight from Hungary due to persecution, subsequently returning from a safe haven to the country of origin where the persecution occurred is not a minor omission and relates to the fundamental underpinning of her claim.

[19] The Appellant alleges that she failed to disclose this information on the advice of former counsel. In rejecting this explanation, the RPD noted that she was represented by experienced counsel who would have been well aware of the biometrics information routinely shared between Canada and the USA Department of Homeland Security and that this error would have eventually come to light. Further to that, I note that there is no evidence that former counsel has been put on notice that such advice might have compromised the Appellant's claim, nor has there been any evidence adduced regarding any form of complaint to the Law Society of Ontario or, for that matter, even to the IRB regarding former counsel's conduct. The Appellant argues that competent and experienced counsel does not necessarily equate to "principled", but allegations such as this are serious and, if accurate, strike at the core of the integrity of the refugee protection system. In the absence of any such evidence regarding former counsel's conduct, I agree with the RPD finding and find it correct that the Appellant's failure to disclose her 7 months' stay in the USA was based on advice from her former counsel undermines her credibility and the credibility of her claim.

[20] The RPD expressed concern that the Appellant had provided a fairly extensive set of medical records, none of which dealt with any of the incidents in which she alleged serious assaultive persecutory conduct had been suffered. In fact, the RPD found that the Appellant had "selectively" provided medical documents.10 I share that concern. For example, the Appellant alleges that in XXXX 2014, a co-worker insulted her by calling her names and then threw some sort of acidic cleaning compound on her leg and shoes. The Appellant claims that she was burned by this compound and required medical care and that it was "cared for for a long time."11 The RPD specifically asked why she did not have medical records to document this incident and the Appellant provided non-responsive, inconsistent and evolving testimony ranging from:
(i) "the police did not come;"
(ii) she did not remember to bring such documents with her;
(iii) "most likely" her ex-husband had them; and
(iv) the fact that "other" doctors (referencing doctors not associated with her XXXX health care) did not care about her.12
Ultimately, the Appellant advised the RPD that it was "necessary to understand that back in Hungary it is so difficult to receive the papers with any direction with the police, including the papers from medical office."13 Not only is the Appellant's testimony in this regard inconsistent and evolving, it flies in the face of the National Documentation Package ("NDP")14 which advises that procedures are available for former patients both within and from out of the country to obtain medical reports.15 While these procedures appear somewhat cumbersome, in light of the Appellant's testimony noted above, I find her various responses to be inadequate and unreasonable and, as a result, draw a negative credibility inference. Once again, mindful of the evidentiary issues noted by Guideline 4, I note that while, perhaps, cumbersome, there is a procedure in existence for obtaining medical reports and the Appellant has not availed herself of that procedure. Accordingly, I find that the Appellant's response(s) to the RPD's questioning as to why she did not obtain the medical reports which would have been corroborative of certain parts of her allegations to be unreasonable.

[21] Similarly, the Appellant claims that one of the incidents where she alleges to have been beaten by "G.S." happened at her parent's home.16 As discussed below, her mother has submitted a letter in support of this allegation that claims the Appellant suffered "serious injuries,"17 yet the Appellant's narrative is silent on any injuries which stemmed from this incident. This is a serious inconsistency in the Appellant's story which again, casts credibility concerns upon her credibility and the credibility of her claim and, as discussed in greater detail below, results in the mother's letter being given no evidentiary weight.
Absence of corroborative material

[22] Other than general country condition type documents, there is little evidence that is corroborative of the specific allegations made in this claim. On the issue of corroboration, I note that the Federal Court in Senadheerage began its analysis with the traditional view that the law of evidence does not require testimony to be corroborated by written documents.18 In Senadheerage, Mr. Justice Grammond points out that the IRB (with good reason) often requires asylum claimants to corroborate their claim with written evidence.19 Reasons for corroboration vary but are rooted in the notion that it is difficult for the Canadian government to investigate events that occurred in another country and requiring corroboration helps ensure that refugee protection is granted to those who deserve it.20 While there are instances and events which may preclude or prevent the gathering of corroborative evidence, " [...] requiring corroboration may be a manner of granting 'fair consideration to those who come to Canada claiming persecution' while 'maintaining the integrity of the Canadian refugee protection system [...]'".21 In making these statements, the Court cautioned that any requirement for corroboration must be "properly calibrated" to avoid putting refugee claimants in an impossible situation.22

[23] The Federal Court also noted that the absence of a general requirement for corroboration is considered a corollary of the Maldonado presumption of truthfulness discussed above which, of course, stands for the proposition that when an applicant swears to the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there be reason to doubt their truthfulness. A competing line of cases would appear to give broader scope to the requirement for corroboration and is sometimes seen as an exception to the rule that, absent credibility concerns, no corroboration is required:
[...] when corroborative evidence should reasonably be available to establish the essential elements of a refugee protection claim and there is no reasonable explanation for its absence, the administrative decision maker may draw a negative inference with respect to credibility based on the claimant's lack of effort to obtain this evidence.23
Ultimately, the Federal Court articulated a somewhat expanded view of corroboration but recognized the risk of corroboration becoming an open-ended requirement. That concern is, quite naturally, of particular importance when considering this claim within the ambit of Guideline 4. However, given the credibility concerns noted, the Appellant's failure to obtain medical reports (when the NDP establishes that such records can be obtained), when considered against her unreasonable explanation for not having those records, undermines the credibility of the claim.
Other corroborative material is not probative

[24] The Appellant has submitted a XXXX report24 indicating that she exhibited symptoms consistent with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.25 The RPD found that it had no probative value and gave it little evidentiary weight.26 This finding was based upon the report being entirely based on the Appellant's self-report, its conclusory comments about the Appellant's credibility, as well as an assessment of the danger she might face and the impact upon her symptoms if returned to Hungary. Moreover, according to the XXXX report, the Appellant's responses to interview questions were "credible and internally consistent". I agree with the RPD that credibility assessment is a fundamental component of the refugee determination process and that, in this regard, the author overstepped her role. Apart from indicating that this assessment was discounted by the RPD because the panel disbelieved the underlying facts on which it was based, the Appellant does not provide any specific allegation as to how the RPD erred in arriving at this conclusion. I note that the report further steps over the line from XXXX to advocate with her comment that her symptoms will increase considerably should she be forced to return to Hungary and references a "history of self-harm"27 for which no evidence has been adduced.

[25] It appears that the report is, in its entirety, based upon the self-report of the Appellant. There is no evidence in the report as to any diagnostic testing which may have been conducted that might verify the conclusions and appears to rely solely upon a one-hour interview. In arriving at the conclusion that the Appellant has suffered from fear, threats, discrimination, physical violence, abuse and trauma, the XXXX once again is exercising one of the functions of the IRB, namely: determination of fact, all based upon the self-report of the Appellant. I also note that, in preparing the report, the XXXX only reviewed the original BOC Narrative and did not review the Amended Narrative which may or may not have had an impact on the report. Based on the foregoing and being guided by the Federal Court in Molefe28 which cautioned against decision-makers giving "exalted status" to such reports (which are largely untested and unverified) I agree with the RPD finding that it has little probative value and, therefore, cannot be assigned evidentiary weight.29

[26] As set out above, the Appellant submitted a letter from her mother,30 purportedly as corroboration of the incidents involving "G.S.". The RPD dismissed the letter on the basis that its authenticity could not be determined. The Appellant argues that this constitutes an error and that certain information provided with the letter would have allowed its authenticity to be established had the RPD chosen to do so. While it may have been within the RPD's ability to further investigate this letter, I find that the letter itself makes certain statements which bring its reliability into question.

[27] The letter reports primarily on an incident which occurred in XXXX 2016 when the Appellant claims that she was beaten by "G.S" at her parents' home. The mother's letter alleges that the Appellant was "physically, brutally assaulted" and suffered "serious injuries" in the incident, however, the Appellant's narrative fails to mention any injuries and, as with the incident involving her co-worker discussed above, she has not provided any medical reports or other corroborating material in support of this allegation. In addition, the mother's letter claims that "G.S." continued to come to their house following this incident and when the Appellant was not present, he assaulted and threatened her parents on several occasions. None of these incidents of assault or threats against her parents are mentioned by the Appellant in either her BOC Narrative, her Amended Narrative or in her testimony. This richness of detail in the mother's letter, as well as the omission of those details from the Appellant's evidence are significant inconsistencies which cause concern for the reliability and accuracy of the letter and I find that I cannot rely on it as an accurate depiction of the event(s) and, albeit for different reasons than the RPD, I find that it is not credible and cannot be given any evidentiary weight.

[28] While RPD Reasons did not comment on this aspect of the letter, the letter is found within the evidentiary record and relates to the credibility of the claim which is (and was) a fundamental component of the claim and the ensuing reasons. As such, I am of the view that this is not a new issue which requires disclosure to the Appellant prior to the rendering of my determination. In this regard, I am informed by the Federal Court decision in Sary31 where evidence that is on the evidentiary record and is not extrinsic to the matter may be reviewed and commented upon by the RAD as part of its independent assessment of the evidence without giving notice to the Appellant.

[29] Similarly, the letter from an organization called the "Rights Protection Association of National Ethnic Minorities of Hungary" is troubling from the standpoint that it relates a great degree of generalization about incidents and is noticeably vague when it comes to detailing such events. Secondly, I find that portion of the letter referencing the police as being "refusing and inactive" in dealing with certain allegations regarding "G.S." particularly troubling. Given the NDP information discussed below regarding robust complaint procedures that have been instituted and the various avenues by which redress might be sought, I find it inconceivable that an organization dedicated to the promotion of rights for Hungarian Roma would simply stand by and allow police inaction without resort to the remedial measures available. This letter is entirely incompatible with the notion of a "rights protection association" and, accordingly, I give it little weight.
Failure to claim in United States/Return to Hungary

[30] The RPD found that the Appellant's failure to claim in the USA impacted upon her claim pointing, once again, to varied and inconsistent explanations for failing to do so.32 The panel found that it was reasonable to expect that a person fleeing persecution and taking flight from the country in which the persecution occurred, finding themselves in a place of safety would at least have made some enquiries or investigated their options. The Appellant argues that failure to claim in a previous country is not always indicative of a lack of subjective fear, provided adequate reasons are given.33 For reasons which follow, I agree with the RPD findings and with the conclusion drawn that her conduct belies the subjective fear element necessary to establish a legitimate refugee claim

[31] More importantly, in my view, the issue of the Appellant having returned to Hungary following her seven months' stay in the USA is a defining point in terms of the intersectionality of her claim. I note that prior to her first departure from Hungary, the nature of the incidents of which she complains in support of her claim relate primarily to discriminatory events she claims to have experienced as a Roma person living and growing up in Hungary. The nature of these complaints is not particularized to her as required by a claim under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Despite these alleged incidents, she chose to return to her country of origin where the original acts of discrimination occurred. While she claimed that she missed her children, there is no disputing the fact that she returned to a country where she claimed to have experienced significant acts of discrimination which, cumulatively, amounted to persecution, from a country in which she was physically safe though, admittedly, her legal status was precarious. I agree with the RPD finding that her failure to claim in the USA, as well as her failure to even investigate making a claim, combined with her subsequent return to Hungary undermine the subjective fear of persecution that is necessary to successfully claim refugee protection, particularly with respect to those events which predate her departure from Hungary.

[32] Following her re-availment to Hungary from the USA, she meets the man who becomes her partner, "G.S." and who she alleges entered into a campaign of persecutory events based upon her Roma ethnicity.

[33] The RPD found that the information dealing with allegations of domestic violence was based solely on that provided by the Appellant34 and that significant credibility concerns undermined her allegations of risk of persecution she would face if return to Hungary.35 While the RPD reasons, in a general sense, address the risk she may face if returned to her country of origin, they fail to specifically address allegations of risk she claims to face from her former partner. I shall endeavour to address and correct that deficiency.

[34] The RPD was correct in its assertion that the allegations of domestic violence at the hand of G.S. is based entirely on the Appellant's testimony. Although the Appellant provided some third-party documentation as corroboration of her claim, I find that these documents fall short of achieving that goal.

[35] By way of example, the Appellant has tendered a letter from a former boyfriend, "V.J.Z.",36 purportedly as evidence of the ongoing risk she faces from G.S. The letter has some evidentiary value as it confirms that an assault took place in 2016, however it fails to address ongoing risk and whether G.S. has the means and motivation to pose a threat almost five years after the event. Moreover, as discussed below in my analysis of state protection, this letter establishes that, on this occasion, the Appellant failed to seek any sort of state protection by failing to report the matter to police because it would have been "humiliating" to V.J.Z.37 As a result, while the letter cannot be discounted entirely, it cannot be given significant weight as it is only marginally probative of the Appellant's allegations regarding G.S. and fails entirely to address the forward-facing risk aspect of the claim.

[36] The Appellant has also submitted correspondence from her brother.38 The contents of this letter are almost exclusively second-hand knowledge and, once again, point to a failure to seek protection by failing to report the incident in which the Appellant claims to have been sexually assaulted by two of G.S.'s friends in 2016. In making this finding, I am sensitive to the dynamics of such assaults and a victim's hesitancy to report but am attempting to balance those concerns against the requirement that a refugee claimant provide proof to a certain standard in order to successfully establish her claim.

[37] The only aspect of this letter by which its author can claim first-hand knowledge is with respect to an alleged 2015 assault (which he did not witness) where the brother claims to have taken the Appellant to a police station only to be laughed at by police who refused to act. The conclusion that he draws, namely: that they were left "with unfathomable disappointment acknowledging that a person of gypsy origin by no means could count on the protection of the authorities and police officers who are corrupt racist and rejoice when gypsies are assaulted"39 runs contrary to the NDP evidence (discussed in greater detail below) and, in that regard, I prefer the objective NDP evidence regarding police training, reporting and the opportunity to report officers who act in a discriminatory fashion.

[38] As a result, as correctly identified by the RPD, the issue of ongoing threat or risk of persecution by G.S. rests entirely upon the Appellant's testimony. Based upon the inconsistencies and credibility concerns which undermined her credibility, the Maldonado presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted and I can come to no other conclusion than the Appellant has failed to discharge her burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the allegations with respect to G.S. took place.
State protection/Forward-looking analysis

[39] The Appellant argues that the RPD did not perform an adequate state protection analysis. I agree that such was the case and that, in performing an inadequate state protection analysis, the RPD erred. The analysis which was performed appears to be limited to the comment that she has had the benefit of some police assistance.40 With respect, the situation in Hungary as it affects persons of Roma ethnicity is much more complex than such a statement might lead one to believe. Regardless of whether past persecution is established or not, the RPD accepted that she is of Roma ethnicity and, as such, that profile requires analysis having regard to the country conditions and her particular facts and circumstances. However, in my role as the "safety net" for the RAD41, I am positioned to conduct a state protection analysis and to correct such error. For reasons which follow, I find that, if returned to Hungary, the Appellant will have access to adequate state protection.
Hungary is a troubled state, but it is not a "failed" state

[40] I shall preface my state protection analysis by saying that I accept the RPD finding that the Appellant is of Roma ethnicity. This fact was established to the RPD's satisfaction through testimony as to particular distinguishing features and characteristics she possesses, as well as certain customs observed by Roma persons. In addition, she produced a letter from the Roma Nationality Self-Government of the Settlement of Megaszo which corroborated her testimony. As such, she has established her Roma ethnicity meaning that she has a residual profile which must be independently assessed in a forward-facing manner as against the country conditions.

[41] Hungary is a democratic state which holds regular elections, is a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the European Union. It is a well-settled law that the greater the level of democracy in a state, the more a claimant must do to exhaust courses of action available. These facts do not warrant a finding that Hungary is capable of offering adequate state protection to its citizens, but they do form part of the equation.

[42] Refugee protection is a form of surrogate protection which is intended to protect a refugee claimant in situations where she has unsuccessfully sought the protection of her country of origin. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might reasonably be forthcoming. There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its own citizens which can only be displaced upon clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens. A state is not required to provide perfect protection and less-than-perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.

[44] As indicated above, it is insufficient to establish that a state is making its "best efforts" or is attempting to make improvements to its domestic situation with respect to the adequacy of state protection. The appropriate test is the test of operational adequacy which involves an assessment as to whether state protection is adequate at the operational level.

[45] The documentary evidence found in the NDP is mixed on the issue of state protection in Hungary and is, perhaps, illustrative of the difficulty in application of the operational adequacy test required by the courts. I note that this evidence is often conflicting and difficult to reconcile, and I am cognizant (as was the RPD) that the documentary evidence shows a history of discrimination against Roma in Hungary. However, as pointed out by the Federal Court in Kotai:
The country conditions do not suggest that the situation is so bleak that all Roma, regardless of their particular circumstances, should not be expected to make reasonable efforts to seek state protection before seeking refugee protection in another country.44
While that comment relates specifically to a situation where an individual may not have made attempts to seek state protection, I also interpret it as a more generalized statement that the country conditions in Hungary are not so dire as to render all Roma persons subject to discrimination amounting to persecution.

[46] The country evidence found in the NDP is clearly mixed and provides information that is both supportive of and contradicts the notion of adequate state protection. For example, the Appellant argues that evidence before the RPD clearly demonstrated that state protection was not reasonably forthcoming for those similarly situated to her.45 I have reviewed the source of the quotation cited by the Appellant and note that this information is immediately followed by information that the Hungarian police, in partnership with the Fraternal Association of European Roma Law Enforcement Officers initiated a project called Initiative for the Improvement of the Police Prevention and Handling of Hate Incidents by which officers from each county were trained on responding to hate crimes within the framework of that project.46

[47] The Appellant also argues that the police refuse to act even when confronted with open and public acts of violence and persecution against Roma citizens.47 In making this argument, an incident in Gyongyospata is referenced where it is alleged that the police failed to protect Roma inhabitants of that town from extremist groups. However, with respect to that particular incident, the NDP also notes that a 2015 court ruling which confirmed that police had, in fact, failed to protect the Roma inhabitants of the village. I find it compelling that this lawsuit was brought by the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union which stated that the ruling, "represents 'a very important achievement, as this is the first Hungarian Court ruling that deems the practice of the police against the Roma to be discriminatory, and therefore unlawful.'"48 [emphasis added]. In my view, this is a clear example where a civil rights "watchdog" has taken action in respect of anti-Roma discriminatory conduct which was recognized as such by the Court which is evidence of state protection. I might add that while one might argue that the notion that the protection of Roma persons is adequate at the operational level because courts have found an initial failure to do so may be illogical and counter-intuitive and does not accord with the notion of adequate state protection, that issue came under review by the Federal Court in Burai.49 Ultimately, the Court was satisfied that incidents such as this were an example of the Hungarian judicial system at work and that it was not unreasonable to rely on such evidence as a reflection of concrete results in terms of state protection."50

[48] In reviewing the documentary evidence, I note that since 2013, the situation has improved for Roma citizens of Hungary;51 the reform is progressing, and positive change has been instituted with concrete results having been achieved. Mindful of my task to differentiate between good intentions or "serious efforts" and actual results, I note that concrete results have been achieved, although it is clear that the pace of these reforms has come under some criticism. For example, the NDP establishes the following:
(i) the European Court of Human Rights ruling that Hungary discriminated against Roma persons when police failed to investigate a 2012 racist attack.52 Once again, as discussed above (and as analyzed by the Federal Court in Burai), decisions such as this represent a positive trend and are concrete results in establishing the operational adequacy of state protection;
(ii) in July 2016, the Hungarian Police, in conjunction with the "Fraternal Association of European Roma Law Enforcement Officers," (an association which aims to promote equal opportunities in law enforcement and to reduce prejudice between law enforcement and Roma Communities),53 initiated a project called "Initiative for the Improvement of the Police Prevention and Handling of Hate Incidents" which resulted in Hungarian police officers from each county receiving specialized training on responding to and investigating hate crimes;54
(iii) a comprehensive complaints process against police and other officials providing government services has been instituted. Although initial complaints are dealt with by the police agency, they can be escalated to an Independent Police Complaints Board. According to the NDP, in the first 9 months of 2014, over 4,000 officers were subject to discipline ranging from imprisonment in the most egregious cases to dismissal to fines and other penalties for less serious offences;55
(iv) the Equal Treatment Authority ("ETA") and the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights are independent bodies established by the Hungarian government. They are tasked with a mandate to receive and deal with individual and public complaints about unequal treatment and ensuring the protection of fundamental rights, respectively. As set out in the NDP, the ETA is active in soliciting complaints and was instrumental in legal action against the city of Miskolc regarding housing discrimination against Roma persons;56
(v) there has been a dedicated effort made in the form of outreach programs designed to recruit police officers from the Roma community and to encourage Roma youth to consider law enforcement as a career. In addition to such recruitment and outreach programs, there have been scholarships granted to Roma youth interested in law enforcement careers, as well as a broad array of other scholarship opportunities for Roma students arising from the National Social Inclusion Policy;57
(vi) legal assistance and support are available for victims of human rights violations and hate crimes;58
(vii) the Equal Treatment Authority ruled in favour of a Romani woman who was harassed with ethnic slurs by hospital staff while giving birth and the hospital was required to publicize the birth and pay a fine;59
(viii) while there are widespread reports of segregation of Roma students in Hungarian schools, the NDP reports that the Metropolitan Court of Budapest delivered a decision that established that the ministry in charge of education was directly responsible for segregation and was ordered to desegregate. A similar decision was upheld by the Appeals Court of Pecs which was affirmed by the Supreme Court.

[49] While the above noted examples, in my view, represent evidence of operational adequacy in Hungary, admittedly the evidence is mixed and, at times, difficult to reconcile. The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance ("ECRI") noted that progress had been made in a number of fields, again citing such gains as amendments to the Criminal Code, the ETA (widely considered a good instrument), the dissolvement of the Hungarian Guard by an appeal court and the setting up of hate crimes units and police monitoring of communications and activities of paramilitary groups and areas at risk of conflict.60 Despite these positive developments, the ECRI noted other issues gave rise to concern and, as noted by the RPD, the Roma of Hungary have experienced discrimination in many aspects of life including health care, education and employment.

[50] Furthermore, the Federal Court has stated that:
[...] suggesting that police oversight agencies have no role in demonstrating adequate state protection is like saying senior policing management has no role in policing due to their oversight function, or saying that policing is a short-term operational exercise...[T]he point is that the evidence in the Hungarian Roma persecution claims indicates that the oversight agencies are diligent in their investigations and in reporting their findings to the police. The transparency and accompanying public criticism of the state protection apparatus is an important ingredient to reforms and improvement in protection services accorded to Roma citizens. [emphasis added]
The requirement to access police oversight agencies is particularly important where the persecution is in the form of random incidents, such as is normally the case for members of the Roma community. Adequate state protection against random crime must operate at a community level over a longer time frame, because responding to any particular victim cannot assure that future random attacks from other assailants will not occur. To the extent that random criminal conduct can be prevented by means other than increased patrols, effective policing can have a deterrent effect by arresting and successfully prosecuting wrongdoers accompanied by the declaratory publicity attached to successful convictions.
Thus, looking ahead, no crime prevention process can be effective if victims of crime do not report incidents to the police and proactively cooperate in their investigations, including complaining if not satisfied with the efforts of the police. If the rhetorical question is whether all members of the Roma community will be better protected from a rule requiring that they follow up with instances of inadequate policing with oversight agencies, I would argue, yes it would. [emphasis added]61

[51] The Appellant has testified that on approximately five occasions, she notified the police about events in which she alleges persecution. One of those occasions was an incident involving her ex-husband who was unable to identify his assailants with the investigation failing to proceed on that basis. In other such circumstances, she claims that she was laughed at by the police who failed to take a report or investigate and the Appellant claims to have (unwillingly) accepted such inaction. In the absence of corroborative material and in light of the credibility concerns, I reject that evidence and prefer the NDP evidence which I find establishes that robust complaints procedures have been enacted and provide recourse for persons, particularly of Roma ethnicity, who suffer such indifference by authorities.

[52] In my view, the Appellant has failed to provide clear and convincing evidence that adequate state protection is not available. Based on Mudrak, while some of the incidents of persecution of which the Appellant complains were random, others appear to have been targeted. Regardless, I note that (as in Mudrak) in at least one of these incidents, the perpetrators could not be identified, and the police investigation went nowhere. In other incidents, the Appellant claims to have contacted police but nothing more which, in my view, indicates that she has not attempted to fully avail herself of the state protection that the Hungarian society has to offer. Having considered her evidence, taking into account the objective NDP evidence and attempting to balance the evidence regarding discrimination against Roma in Hungary, I must give more weight to the NDP evidence which, though conflicting, supports the notion that Hungary, though a troubled state, is a state which is capable of providing the Appellant with adequate state protection should she be returned there.
Summary

[53] As discussed above, the Appellant's claim features an intersectionality between her claim as a Hungarian Roma and her claim as a Hungarian Roma woman claiming gender-related persecution at the hands of her former partner. Though it is not possible to neatly dissect the two aspects of her claim as there is a certain degree of overlap, it can be notionally segmented into two distinct phases: the first phase being prior to her departure from Hungary for the USA in 2012 and the second phase commencing with her subsequent return in 2013. Her failure to claim refugee status in the USA and her return to Hungary has been found to undermine the subjective fear element necessary to support a successful refugee claim, particularly with events that pre-dated her departure from her country of origin. Following re-availment to Hungary, she became involved with her partner, "G.S." who she claims became abusive to her because of her Roma ethnicity. The evidence featured a number of credibility concerns that have been highlighted and which cast doubt upon the credibility of her claim. While corroborative material may have been readily available in the form of medical reports relating to particular incidents, none was provided, and the Appellant provided unreasonable and/or inconsistent and evolving explanations for not having such reports which resulted in adverse credibility findings. Such corroborative material that was provided could not be given any evidentiary weight due to reliability concerns. In addition, the Appellant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the incidents involving "G.S." occurred. The Appellant has the onus to provide clear and convincing evidence that adequate state protection is unavailable to her and, on a balance of probabilities, has failed to do so.
CONCLUSION

[54] Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
